dispatch.headline: Mourners Told To Hum
dispatch.body:
Priya Nair wiped bright teal mould onto her uncle's urn shelf on Friday afternoon.

She is one of hundreds of young residents across Marius Basin applying bio-reactive grave spores to family crypts. Cultured in kitchen sinks, the fungus produces vivid neon rings across the basalt vaults.

It looks tidy.

The municipal burial board is currently receiving furious delegations from elder guilds after the spores colonised the dome's central misting grid. The growth binds to dental enamel through ordinary tap water. During Tuesday's dim-room memorial for a district pipe-fitter, forty mourners opened their mouths for the opening hymn and lit the chapel in electric green.

"People were trying to grieve," said guild warden Hideo Sato, whose own teeth cast a lime beam across his lapel during the service. "Then the choir opened up. You could see right down their throats. It was like looking into a pair of high-beams."

Asked whether the pumps could be flushed before the next wake, water supervisor Aris Thorne said the pipes held eighty thousand tonnes of fluid, and that this was simply the colour of the water now.

Officiants have advised future congregations to hum, though early trials suggest a low baritone still causes the nostrils to pulse like emergency beacons.
dispatch.scene: A mourner in a dark grey tunic sits with his lips pressed tightly shut in a dim chapel while bright green light leaks between his teeth, two relatives staring beside him.

glossary.gloss: A bio-reactive domestic fungus cultured in greywater, popular among younger citizens for decorating basalt family crypts with vivid neon rings.

dispatch.premise: Young lunar residents are using bioluminescent tomb-fungus to make family graves glow in trendy neon colors, an aesthetic that elders decry now that the highly adaptive spores have colonised the dome's water supply and made everyone's teeth glow during municipal funerals.

brief.setting: a dim, windowless municipal crypt built from dark, hexagonal fused-basalt blocks, with two relatives in dark formal drapes sitting beside him on a composite bench, staring at his face
brief.light: weak, cool light from a recessed ceiling panel, contrasted by the sharp, self-luminous green beam projecting from the mouth

brief.anomaly: a small, cylindrical personal air-filter cartridge with a scuffed casing set down on the bench next to his thigh

drafts.headline: Mourners Told To Keep Mouths Closed
drafts.body:
Priya Nair wiped bright teal mould onto her uncle's urn shelf on Friday afternoon.

She is one of hundreds of young residents across Marius Basin applying bio-reactive grave spores to family crypts. The fungus, cultured in domestic greywater drains, produces vivid neon rings across the basalt vaults.

It looks tidy.

The municipal burial board now faces formal complaints from elder guilds after the spores colonised the dome's central misting grid. The growth binds naturally to dental enamel through ordinary tap water. During Tuesday's dim-room memorial for a district pipe-fitter, forty mourners opened their mouths to sing and lit the chapel in electric green.

Elders called it disrespectful.

"People were trying to grieve," said guild warden Hideo Sato, whose own teeth cast a lime beam across his lapel. "Then the choir opened up. You could see right down their throats."

Asked whether the pumps could be cleaned before the next wake, water supervisor Aris Thorne said the pipes held eighty thousand tonnes of fluid, and that this was the colour of the water now.

Officiants have advised future congregations to hum through closed lips.

quality.critique: The previous headline was a bit dry and merely descriptive rather than punchy. The ending lacked a sharp comedic escalation of the glowing-teeth premise.
